classification.difficultyReason: Uses the supplied stars-and-bars model to count a concrete distribution, then generalises the correspondence to n items and r recipients.

content.prompt: Suppose there are 6 identical lollies and 3 students, A, B and C. The lollies are to be distributed amongst the students. Not all students need to be given lollies. The stars and bars below show a way to distribute the lollies such that A gets 2, B gets 1, C gets 3.

spec.description: Six black stars separated by two vertical bars into groups of two, one and three.
spec.mathematics: Left-to-right allocations to A, B and C are 2, 1 and 3.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent supplied illustration, visible in the student edition.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many ways are there of distributing the lollies amongst the 3 students?

answer.worked:
This is equivalent to arranging 6 identical stars and 2 identical bars.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of ways}&=\frac{8!}{6!2!}\\&=28.\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, choose 2 of the 8 positions for the bars: $\binom{8}{2}=28$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence prove that there are $\binom{n+r-1}{n}$ ways to distribute $n$ identical items amongst $r$ people, allowing people to receive no items.

answer.worked:
Represent the $n$ identical items by $n$ stars and separate the allocations to the $r$ people, in a fixed order, using $r-1$ bars. Adjacent bars or bars at either end allow people to receive no items. Each arrangement corresponds to exactly one distribution, and conversely.
There are $n+r-1$ positions. Choose the $r-1$ positions occupied by bars:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of distributions}&=\binom{n+r-1}{r-1}\\&=\binom{n+r-1}{n},\end{aligned}$$
using the symmetry property of combinations.
